name: Mare
description: Maren (the Mare) is the Danish nightmare spirit — a female entity who sits on sleeping people's chests, pressing the air from their lungs and causing terrifying dreams. In Danish folklore, the Mare is a shape-shifter who can take the form of a cat, a dog, an owl, a horse, or even a straw. She is blamed for sleep paralysis, which in Danish is called 'mare-reden' (mare-ride). The Mare creates 'marelokker' (mare-locks) — tangled knots in horses' manes and women's hair, believed to be where she has been braiding at night. Protection against the Mare includes placing steel in the bed, reversing shoes before sleeping, carving a pentagram (called a 'marekors' or mare-cross) over the door, or sprinkling flax seeds on the floor — the Mare must count every seed before she can approach In Denmark folklore, this figure is known among the Denmark people.
source: Danish folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Maria Makiling (Mariang Makiling)
description: Maria Makiling is the most famous diwata (nature spirit/goddess) in Philippine mythology, the guardian spirit of Mount Makiling in Laguna. She is a breathtakingly beautiful young woman with long black hair and radiant white clothing who protects the mountain's forests, wildlife, and the people who depend on them. Pre-colonially venerated as the goddess Dayang Masalanta, she was sent by the supreme deity Bathala to aid mankind. She rewards those who respect nature and punishes those who harm it. Legends tell of her turning ginger into gold to help the poor, guiding lost hikers, and appearing as a vision of serene beauty to those pure of heart. Her spurned love for mortals who betrayed her is said to be why she now hides from human sight, only appearing as wisps of cloud around the mountain's peak
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Makiling

name: Marmæle
description: Marmæle (also called marmennil) is a small prophetic merman in Norwegian folklore, first described in Konungs skuggsjá (The King's Mirror, c. This child-sized, half-human half-fish creature was believed to dwell in the deep waters off the coast of Norway, particularly along the Vestlandet fjords. Fishermen who caught a marmæle could force it to foretell the future — it would predict weather, fish catches, and the fates of those present. The marmæle was considered a type of sjøvette (sea wight) and was more benevolent than the sjødraug. It was said to have the upper body of a tiny man with webbed hands and a fish-like lower body. Capturing one was considered bad luck unless it was released after three days. The marmæle tradition appears in Icelandic Landnámabók as well, where a captured marmennil prophesied about the settlement of Iceland
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Marmennil
description: Marmennil (Marmennilin) is a mischievous merman from Faroese folklore who lives at the bottom of the sea near Elduvík on Eysturoy. Smaller than a human with abnormally long fingers, he delights in teasing fishermen by biting bait off hooks and snagging lines to the seabed. The most famous legend tells of farmer Anfinn (Andfind Jacobsen, born c. 1575), who accidentally hooked Marmennil's hand while fishing and pulled him into the boat. The fishermen made the sign of the cross and brought Marmennil home, where Anfinn kept him by the fireplace for years. Whenever fish were beneath the boat, Marmennil would laugh and play, and the men always caught plenty. But one day in rough surf, the men forgot to make the sign of the cross, and Marmennil escaped into the sea forever. A bronze statue by Hans Pauli Olsen was unveiled in Elduvík on 23 August 2020 to commemorate the legend
source: Faroese folklore; mermen are known from local maritime legends and narratives.

name: Matsyendranath (Karunamaya)
description: Matsyendranath, also known as Karunamaya ('the compassionate one') and Red Machindranath, is one of the most important deities in Nepali Buddhism and Hinduism, revered as the god of rain and compassion. The central legend tells of a devastating 12-year drought that struck the Kathmandu Valley, caused by the demon Bhasmasura (or Bhasmasur). The powerful yogi Gorakhnath had captured all the nagas (serpent gods) in meditation, blocking the rainfall. The people, led by the king of Bhadgaon, traveled to Assam to seek help from Matsyendranath, Gorakhnath's guru. When Matsyendranath arrived in the valley, his mere presence forced Gorakhnath to release the nagas, bringing life-giving rain and restoring the valley to fertility. Matsyendranath is revered as an avatar of Avalokiteshvara (Padmapani), the bodhisattva of compassion. His connection to the revived Red Machindranath chariot festival in Patan — one of Nepal's oldest and grandest processions — involves transporting his towering chariot through the streets of Patan for a month-long festival that is central to Newar cultural identity
source: Swayambhu Purana, Nepali Buddhist/Hindu traditions, Patan festival records

name: Máttaráhkká
description: Máttaráhkká is a goddess from Sami mythology. She lives in the ground beneath the goahti, opposite the door in the maadtere (women's sacred space). She is the great ancestress who receives the human soul from Radien-attje and gives it life before passing it to her daughter Sáráhkká who places it in the womb. She makes female humans and animals fertile. Her name literally means 'origin woman' or 'ancestral mother.' According to Christfried Ganander (1789), she receives the child from Radien-attje, breathes life into it, then hands it to Sáráhkká. Some sources give her a husband, Máttaráhttje, but he has a much smaller role and is considered a later addition. She and her three daughters (Sáráhkká, Juoksáhkká, Uksáhkká) form the core group of Sami domestic goddesses. On the Kola Peninsula, the Sami used the word mändir-ähke meaning 'parent's grandmother,' suggesting she was originally a female ancestor buried in the ground and worshipped by later generations
source: Wikipedia (Máttaráhkká); baalka.se; Brooklyn Museum; saamelaisensyklopedia.fi

name: Maya Mriga (Golden Deer)
description: The Maya Mriga (Golden Deer) is a pivotal illusionary creature from the Ramayana, created by the rakshasa Maricha at Ravana's command. To enable Ravana's abduction of Sita, Maricha transformed himself into a mesmerizing golden deer with silver spots and jewel-like horns that appeared to be made of precious metals and gems. The deer's magical beauty was so captivating that Sita, seeing it near their forest hermitage, asked Rama to capture it for her. Despite Lakshmana's warnings that such a creature could not be natural and was likely a trick, Rama pursued the deer deep into the forest. The golden deer led Rama far from the hermitage, then, as it died from Rama's arrow, mimicked Rama's voice calling for help — 'O Lakshmana! O Sita!' — a desperate cry that drew Lakshmana away from Sita, leaving her vulnerable to Ravana. The Maya Mriga thus represents illusion (maya) used as a weapon, and its role is the catalyst for the central conflict of the Ramayana
source: Valmiki Ramayana (Aranya Kanda), various Ramayana adaptations

name: Mbidi Kiluwe
description: Mbidi Kiluwe is the legendary culture hero and founding father of Luba sacred kingship (bulopwe). According to Luba oral tradition, Mbidi Kiluwe was a mysterious prince from the east, distinguished by his refined, dignified manners. He arrived at the court of King Nkongolo Mwamba, the crude and violent red-skinned ruler. Where Nkongolo was barbaric, Mbidi Kiluwe was gentle and wise. He introduced civilizing customs: eating in private, using utensils, speaking softly, covering one's face with dignity. Mbidi Kiluwe married Nkongolo's sister Bulanda, but was forced to flee when Nkongolo's tyranny became unbearable. Before leaving, he prophesied his unborn son would overthrow Nkongolo. Mbidi Kiluwe's refined manners became the model for Luba kingship (bulopwe), establishing sacred traditions defining Luba royal culture for centuries
source: Luba oral tradition, Mbudye historians, Encyclopaedia Africana, tianmu.org

name: Mbona
description: Mbona is a legendary rain-bringing prophet and martyr from Chewa and Mang'anja mythology of Malawi. Unlike purely mythical figures, Mbona may be based on a historical figure who lived around the 16th century. According to tradition, Mbona possessed extraordinary magic powers: he could bring rain during droughts, create wells of water in sandy lands, cause forests to appear where none existed, and hide from his enemies by transforming into other creatures such as guinea fowls. Mbona's powers made him both beloved by his people and feared by his enemies. Nabbed by his rivals, he was decapitated, but his head continued to speak and prophesy even after his death. His grave became a sacred site, and the Mbona cult remains active in Malawi to this day, with his spirit speaking through mediums. The most famous shrine dedicated to Mbona is at Khulubvi in southern Malawi, where annual ceremonies are held to petition for rain and good harvests. The site is considered so sacred that entry is restricted to certain days and requires specific rituals
source: iplmyths.blogspot.com; Chewa oral traditions

name: Meandash
description: Meandash is the mythic wild reindeer of eastern Sami (Kola Peninsula) tradition, a shapeshifter who is human inside his hut and a reindeer outside. He is the central culture hero of the Ter and Kildin Sami, credited with teaching humans the art of hunting and gifting them the bow. Nearly 30 stories about Meandash have been recorded. He was born to a female noaidi (shaman) who conceived him in reindeer form from a wild reindeer. Meandash lives in a hut made of reindeer skin and bones, separated from the human world by a river of blood with lungs for waves and livers for stones. He marries an earthly girl who crosses this river, and they have children born human. When his wife breaks a taboo by drying urine-soaked reindeer skins in the sun, Meandash transforms permanently into a wild reindeer, and his children become reindeer calves, forming the first wild reindeer herds. In a later act of self-sacrifice, Meandash allows himself to be killed by a Sami hunter so his meat can feed the people, thereby teaching them hunting skills
source: folklore.ee/vol11/meandash.htm; saamelaisensyklopedia.fi; Charnoluskij recordings

name: Midnight Robber (Trinidad Carnival Mas Character)
description: The Midnight Robber is one of the most iconic and beloved traditional masquerade characters of Trinidad and Tobago Carnival. He is a bombastic, theatrical outlaw who combines the swagger of a Wild West gunslinger with the oratory tradition of a West African griot (storyteller). He wears an oversized wide-brimmed hat (often shaped like a coffin or a crown), a flowing black cape decorated with symbols of death and destruction (skulls, crossbones), black satin shirt and pantaloons, and carries a wooden money box shaped like a coffin, a dagger or pistol, and a whistle. His signature feature is Robber Talk -- an elaborate, grandiose monologue delivered in a deep voice, mixing Shakespearean English, biblical cadences, and Creole. He boasts of his invincible ancestry, his terrifying exploits, and his plans for vengeance against his enemies. He stops passersby, holds them at ransom with his eloquence, and demands money before releasing them. The Midnight Robber first appeared in Trinidad Carnival in the early 1900s, drawing from American Wild West imagery and African griot storytelling
source: Trinidadian oral tradition, Trinidad and Tobago folklore

name: Migoi (Bhutanese Yeti)
description: The Migoi (from Tibetan 'mi rgod' meaning 'wild man') is Bhutan's indigenous version of the Yeti, a magical wild creature inhabiting the high Himalayan pastures and deep forests. Unlike the more physical Nepali Yeti, the Bhutanese Migoi possesses supernatural qualities: it can become invisible at will, its blood has magical properties used for talismans, and it carries two enchanted objects — the dipshing (a juniper twig that grants invisibility) and the sem phatsa (a special satchel without which it loses all power). Bhutanese folklore distinguishes between two types: the mechume, a smaller ape-like being with reddish-brown hair that inhabits deep forests, and the gredpo (or migoi proper), a huge creature with grayish-black hair said to have a hollow back — a feature associated with dangerous ghosts. The Migoi is considered a bad omen, and only certain spiritually gifted people can see it. Its habitat is so respected that the Sakteng Wildlife Sanctuary in eastern Bhutan was established in part to protect the Migoi's habitat, making it possibly the only wildlife sanctuary in the world designated partly for a legendary creature
source: Kunzang Choden 'Bhutanese Tales of the Yeti', Sakteng Wildlife Sanctuary records, Bhutanese oral folklore

name: Mocko Jumbie
description: The Mocko Jumbie is a towering stilt-walking spirit dancer and a central figure in St. Kitts and Nevis Carnival and folklore traditions. The name combines 'Moko' (a West African deity who guards, heals, and delivers retribution) and 'Jumbie' (a Caribbean spirit). Dressed in colorful flowing costumes and balancing on 6-to-8-foot stilts, Mocko Jumbies are believed to be ancestral spirits who walk among the living, providing protection and warding off evil. The tradition was brought to St. Kitts by enslaved Africans and has been preserved for over 200 years. In Kittitian culture, Mocko Jumbies appear during Christmas and Carnival celebrations, and their towering height symbolizes the power of God and the ability to see evil before it reaches the community. The tradition was documented in St. Kitts as early as the late 18th century
source: St. Kitts and Nevis oral tradition; snip SKNIS; snip SKNVibes; snip Department of Creative Economy

name: Mokele-Mbembe
description: Mokele-Mbembe is a dragon from Bantu mythology. This cryptid is described as a large, reptilian creature resembling a sauropod dinosaur with a long, flexible neck and a single horn or tooth. Stories of the creature have been told for centuries among the Bantu peoples of Central Africa, including the Ba'Aka, whose oral traditions speak of a beast that lurks in deep river pools and swamps. During the early 20th century, European explorers and cryptozoologists brought the legend to global attention, leading to over fifty expeditions searching for evidence. While most scientists believe the stories stem from misidentified rhinoceroses, large snakes, or folk memory of once-extant megafauna, the mokele-mbembe remains one of Africa's most famous cryptids. In recent years, deforestation and habitat loss have led to increased reported sightings as displaced wildlife is mistaken for the legendary creature
source: Bantu/Lingala oral tradition and cryptozoological literature

name: Mokele-Mbembe
aliases: One Who Stops the Flow of Rivers
description: Mokele-Mbembe, meaning 'one who stops the flow of rivers' in the Lingala language, is a legendary water-dwelling entity from Bantu mythology of the Congo River Basin. This cryptid is described as a large, reptilian creature resembling a sauropod dinosaur with a long, flexible neck and a single horn or tooth. Stories of the creature have been told for centuries among the Bantu peoples of Central Africa, including the Ba'Aka, whose oral traditions speak of a beast that lurks in deep river pools and swamps. During the early 20th century, European explorers and cryptozoologists brought the legend to global attention, leading to over fifty expeditions searching for evidence. While most scientists believe the stories stem from misidentified rhinoceroses, large snakes, or folk memory of once-extant megafauna, the mokele-mbembe remains one of Africa's most famous cryptids. In recent years, deforestation and habitat loss have led to increased reported sightings as displaced wildlife is mistaken for the legendary creature
source: Central African cryptozoology — the Mokele-mbembe is a dinosaur-like cryptid documented in Congolese oral tradition.

name: Moskkjerringa
description: Moskkjerringa (the Moskenes Old Woman) is a female troll of Moskenesøy in Lofoten, turned to stone and overlooking the Moskenesstraumen — the famous maelstrom or tidal whirlpool between Moskenesøy and Værøy islands. The rock formation of an old woman sits on the cliffs above the powerful tidal current. Moskkjerringa is said to have been a female jøtul or troll-woman who was fishing when the sun rose, freezing her in place with her fishing line still in the water. The Moskenesstraumen maelstrom is one of the world's strongest tidal currents, described by Edgar Allan Poe in his story A Descent into the Maelström. The Moskkjerringa rock formation warns sailors of the dangerous waters below. The legend ties together the dramatic sea conditions and the rock formation into a single story of a troll-woman caught by the sun while fishing
source: Scandinavian folklore; trolls are pervasive anthropomorphic beings in Nordic myths, documented in laestadian and ethnographic records.

name: Mouros
description: Supernatural beings in Portuguese and Galician mythology, believed to be an ancient race that inhabited the land since the beginning of time before being forced underground for unknown reasons. The Mouros work gold, silver, and gemstones in subterranean forges beneath hills and ancient castro settlements, guarding enormous treasures protected by dragon-like cuélebres. They rarely emerge except to obtain food and during special liminal times like Midsummer (São João). Some appear as giants or warriors, while others take tiny forms called Mourinhos or Maruxinhos. The Moura Encantada (enchanted Moor woman) is their most famous manifestation. They are associated with megalithic monuments, and archaeologists have used Mouro legends to locate archaeological sites In Portugal folklore, this figure is known among the Portugal people.
source: Galician/Portuguese mythology; the Mouros are an ancient race of supernatural beings.

name: Máttaráhkká
description: Máttaráhkká (Origin Woman) is the primordial mother goddess in Sami shamanism, the most ancient of the female divinities. She lives in the ground beneath the goahti, opposite the door in the maadtere (women's sacred space). She is the great ancestress who receives the human soul from Radien-attje and gives it life before passing it to her daughter Sáráhkká who places it in the womb. She makes female humans and animals fertile. Her name literally means 'origin woman' or 'ancestral mother.' According to Christfried Ganander (1789), she receives the child from Radien-attje, breathes life into it, then hands it to Sáráhkká. Some sources give her a husband, Máttaráhttje, but he has a much smaller role and is considered a later addition. She and her three daughters (Sáráhkká, Juoksáhkká, Uksáhkká) form the core group of Sami domestic goddesses. On the Kola Peninsula, the Sami used the word mändir-ähke meaning 'parent's grandmother,' suggesting she was originally a female ancestor buried in the ground and worshipped by later generations
source: Sami mythology; the primordial mother goddess Mttarhkk, documented in Sami spiritual records.

name: Máttaráhkká
description: Máttaráhkká is a goddess from Sápmi mythology. She lives in the ground beneath the goahti, opposite the door in the maadtere (women's sacred space). She is the great ancestress who receives the human soul from Radien-attje and gives it life before passing it to her daughter Sáráhkká who places it in the womb. She makes female humans and animals fertile. Her name literally means 'origin woman' or 'ancestral mother.' According to Christfried Ganander (1789), she receives the child from Radien-attje, breathes life into it, then hands it to Sáráhkká. Some sources give her a husband, Máttaráhttje, but he has a much smaller role and is considered a later addition. She and her three daughters (Sáráhkká, Juoksáhkká, Uksáhkká) form the core group of Sami domestic goddesses. On the Kola Peninsula, the Sami used the word mändir-ähke meaning 'parent's grandmother,' suggesting she was originally a female ancestor buried in the ground and worshipped by later generations
source: Sami mythology; the primordial mother goddess Mttarhkk, documented in Sami spiritual records.

name: Myromskåna
description: Myromskåna (the Bog Woman) is a female marsh spirit from Setesdal folklore in Sørlandet. The myromskåna dwells in the extensive bogs and marshes of the Setesdal valley floor and leads travelers astray into dangerous mires. She appears as an old woman dressed in grey rags, often beckoning for help from the edge of the bog. When someone approaches to assist, she leads them deeper into the marsh until they become trapped in the quicksand-like mire. The myromskåna is distinct from the more general Norwegian skrømt in that she is specifically a female bog spirit, not a shapeless apparition. She is also distinct from the hulder — she does not seduce but rather deceives through pity. She was particularly feared by travelers crossing the marshy areas of Setesdal, where the valley bottom is prone to flooding and bog formation. Johannes Skar cataloged myromskåna in his collection of Setesdal folk belief as a distinct being of the wetlands
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Nøstekatt
description: Nøstekatt (also naustkatt, from naust = boathouse) is a spirit cat that lives in boathouses (naust) along the Vestlandet coast. The nøstekatt is a supernatural cat that guards the fishing gear and boats stored in the naust. It appears as a large grey or black cat that is never seen outside the boathouse. The nøstekatt protects fishing equipment from thieves and supernatural harm, but also steals small quantities of fish for itself. Fishermen who kept their gear in a naust with a nøstekatt would always have good luck at sea. However, offending the nøstekatt — by being wasteful with fish, neglecting gear, or disrespecting the boathouse — would result in lost catches, damaged nets, and bad weather. The nøstekatt was believed to be the spirit of a drowned fisherman's cat, or in some versions, the cat that lived on the boat and was lost at sea with its owner. The tradition is particularly strong in the fishing communities of Hordaland and Sogn og Fjordane
source: Norwegian folklore, collected by Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe

name: Nainas
description: Nainas is a Sami mythological figure associated with the Northern Lights (Aurora Borealis). In Sami tradition, the Northern Lights are sometimes seen as warrior spirits or celestial beings, and Nainas embodies this concept. In the romantic Sami folk tale 'The Daughter of the Moon and the Son of the Sun,' Nainas leads a band of Northern Light warriors who enter an empty house by the sea at dusk. When the Sun sees Nainas and pins him with a heat shaft, the Moon's daughter Niekia shields Nainas and is seized by the Sun. The Moon rescues her daughter, and Niekia ultimately chooses love with the Northern Lights (Nainas) over the Sun's son Peivalke. This story portrays Nainas as a heroic, romantic figure — the personification of the aurora as a beautiful and powerful warrior. In broader Sami tradition, the Northern Lights were treated with both awe and fear — some believed they were the souls of the dead playing ball with a walrus skull, and one should not whistle at them or they would descend and carry you away
source: Sami folk tale; freebooksforkids.net; illustrated by E. Bulatov and O. Vasiliev

name: Namdalsdraugen
description: Namdalsdraugen (the Namdalen Draug) is a sea draug specific to the Namdalen coast and the Namsenfjorden area of northern Trøndelag. Namdalen has a long and rich fishing tradition, and the Namdalsdraugen is the embodiment of the dangers of the Namdalen coast, one of the most treacherous stretches of water in Norway. The Namdalsdraugen is said to be the combined spirit of all those who have drowned in the Namsenfjorden and along the Namdalen coast. Unlike a single draug, the Namdalsdraugen can appear in multiple places at once, a reflection of the many shipwrecks in this area. It appears as a half-human, half-seaweed figure with glowing eyes, sitting on the rocks or floating just beneath the surface. When the Namdalsdraugen is seen, it means someone will drown within three days. The only way to protect oneself is to carry a piece of iron or to draw a cross on the boat's prow. The legend is strongest in the fishing villages of Namsos, Osen, Flatanger, and Vikna
source: Norse mythology; Draugar are undead spirits of the dead, documented in the Sagas and Nordic folklore.

name: Nanabolele
aliases: They Who Shine in the Night
description: The Nanabolele are horrid, reptilian creatures from Basotho mythology that live underwater and underground in the Lesotho highlands. Their most distinctive feature is their ability to glow in the darkness, giving off a luminous light similar to that of the moon and stars. These creatures are often described as a type of water-dwelling reptile or serpent with bioluminescent properties, making them both beautiful and terrifying. According to legend, the nanabolele skin, which shines in the dark, was highly prized by the Basotho people. The most famous story tells of a brave woman named Thakane who, along with her brothers, hunted the nanabolele, cutting and preparing their glowing skin into clothing, armor, and weapons that would provide light in the darkness. The nanabolele are associated with the dark, cold waters of Lesotho's rivers and mountain streams, and they represent the hidden dangers and mysterious beauty of the underwater world
source: A Book of Creatures; Basotho oral traditions

name: Nang Kwak (Cat-Calling Prosperity Goddess)
description: Nang Kwak (Thai: นางกวัก) is a benevolent female deity in Thai folklore who brings good fortune, prosperity, and customers to businesses. She is depicted as a beautiful woman in traditional Thai dress, seated with her right hand raised in a beckoning gesture — the 'cat-calling' wave that draws customers and wealth. According to legend, Nang Kwak was a virtuous woman who was granted supernatural powers by the Buddha to attract wealth and abundance. Her origins connect to pre-Buddhist Tai folk religion and spirit traditions of Siam. Nearly every shop, restaurant, and business in Thailand displays a statue of Nang Kwak near the entrance. Her imagery is also linked to Suvannamaccha, the golden mermaid from the Thai Ramakien epic. The legend teaches that prosperity comes not from greed but from kindness, hard work, and generosity
source: Thai folklore, Tai folk religion, Phraya Anuman Rajadhon's studies

name: Neang Neak (Queen Soma / Naga Princess)
description: Neang Neak (Khmer: នាងនាគ, 'Dragon Woman'), also known as Queen Soma, is the legendary Naga serpent princess who became the first queen of Cambodia. According to Khmer founding myth, she was the beautiful daughter of the Naga king who ruled the underwater realm. She confronted the Indian Brahmin prince Preah Thong (Kaundinya) on the shore, and after being struck by his magic arrow, fell in love and agreed to marry him. Her father the Naga king blessed the union and drained the ocean to create land for their kingdom — the birth of Cambodia. Neang Neak represents the indigenous, matrilineal, and animist foundation of Khmer civilization. She is considered the matriarch of the Khmer people, and her serpent lineage explains the importance of the naga in Cambodian culture. The tradition of the groom holding the bride's sash during Khmer weddings reenacts Preah Thong holding Neang Neak's tail as he descended to the Naga kingdom
source: Khmer royal chronicles, Chinese historical records (Kang Tai, Zhu Ying)

name: Nerstenhornets underjordiske
description: Nerstenhornets underjordiske is a supernatural being from the burial mounds at Nersten farm in Øyestad, near Arendal. According to Andreas Faye's Norske Sagn (1833), a large farmer named Sjur was riding past burial mounds at Lia near Temsevannet when an underground being emerged and offered him a magnificent drinking horn. Sjur threw the drink over his shoulder — the drink burned the hide off his horse. He galloped away with the horn. He was only saved from the pursuing being because he rode over a rye field, which the being could not cross. The horn became known as Nerstenhornet. This legend is one of Sørlandet's 21 variants of the classic horn-stealing legend type. The being from the Nersten mound is distinct from the Ime variant — it emerged specifically from a burial mound near a lake and could not cross a cultivated rye field, reflecting the agricultural landscape of Øyestad
source: Norway mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Nidaros-Munken
description: Nidaros-Munken (the Monk of Nidaros) is a famous ghost that haunts Nidaros Cathedral in Trondheim. The specter is said to be a Catholic monk from the cathedral's pre-Reformation days who was killed during the Reformation turmoil of 1537. The ghost appears as a tall, hooded figure in a black or brown monk's habit, often with a bloody wound on its neck or head. It has been seen walking silently through the cathedral nave, kneeling at the main altar, and disappearing through stone walls. Some versions describe it as headless, carrying its own head. The ghost is most active during Christmas and on the anniversary of the Reformation. It is considered one of Norway's most famous church ghosts and is well documented in Trondheim's local folklore tradition. The Nidaros Cathedral was the most important church in medieval Norway, making its ghost legend particularly significant
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Nidelv-Nøkken
description: Nidelv-Nøkken (the Nidelva Nixie) is a localized version of the nøkk (water spirit) that specifically inhabits the Nidelva river in Trondheim. The Nidelva flows through the heart of Trondheim, from Selbusjøen to the Trondheimsfjord, passing under several bridges and through the city center. According to Trondheim folklore, the Nidelv-Nøkken lives in the deep pool beneath Bakke bru (Bakke Bridge), where the water is darkest and deepest. The spirit takes the form of a beautiful horse that emerges from the river at night — the classic bäckahästen (brook horse) tradition — luring people to ride it and then galloping into the deepest part of the river. The Nidelv-Nøkken is also known to appear as a handsome young man playing a fiddle on the riverbank at night, his music irresistible to passersby who are drawn toward the water. The legend was particularly used to warn children away from the dangerous river currents in the city center
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Nile Water Spirits (Nilotic Folk Belief)
description: The Nile water spirits are a class of supernatural beings in Egyptian folk belief who inhabit the Nile River and its canals, lakes, and irrigation channels. Unlike the singular Sheikh of the Nile, these are numerous spirits that live in specific sections of the river, each with its own territory and characteristics. They are considered a type of jinn in Islamic Egyptian contexts. Some are benevolent, helping fishermen find good catches and protecting children from drowning; snip others are malicious, dragging swimmers to their deaths or capsizing boats. They are most active at night, dawn, and during the flood season. Offerings of bread, dates, or milk are left at riverbanks to gain their favor. They are shape-shifters, often appearing as beautiful women, giant fish, or luminous figures on the water
source: Egyptian folklore, rural Upper Egyptian traditions

name: Nis Puk
description: Nis Puk (also called Puge) is a household spirit from Sønderjylland and the Danish-German border region, a variant of the Nisse but with distinct traits. Nis Puk is short and broad, wears red trousers and a red pointed cap, and lives in the barn or stable of a farm. His special talent is stealing grain and fodder from neighboring farms to enrich his own host farm — a form of supernatural redistribution that made him popular with farmers but feared by neighbors. Nis Puk can carry entire barn-loads of hay on his back and can transform into a cat or a fiery dragon. He also has the power to stop bridal processions and make the horses rear, and wood shavings he scatters turn to gold. Unlike the relatively benign Nisse, Nis Puk is mischievous and demanding — requiring a bowl of porridge with a pat of butter every Thursday evening
source: Denmark mythology, oral tradition & folklore collections

name: Nix
description: Nix is a water-spirit from Germanic/Nordic mythology. Similar to the Celtic kelpie, the Swiss Nix can assume multiple forms—most commonly a beautiful woman who lures men to watery deaths, but also a horse, fish, or even a log. According to Swiss folklore collected in central Switzerland, the Nix has complete control over water and weather, capable of causing floods or droughts at will. In some tales from Lake Lucerne, the Nix is a malevolent ghost that drowns anyone who pollutes or disrupts its underwater domain. However, in traditions from the Bernese Oberland, the Nix is more ambivalent—sometimes helping fishermen in exchange for offerings of bread or milk. The Nix's song is said to be hauntingly beautiful, heard on misty mornings over still lakes. Fishermen along Lake Zurich traditionally left the first catch of the day as an offering to appease the Nix before it claimed their lives
source: Germanic and Nordic folklore, Scandinavian oral traditions

Similar to the Celtic kelpie, the Swiss Nix can assume multiple forms—most commonly a beautiful woman who lures men to watery deaths, but also a horse, fish, or even a log. name: Nøkk
description: Nøkk (also known as Nøkken, Näcken, Nykkjen) is a male freshwater spirit in Norwegian and Scandinavian folklore who dwells in dark lakes, rivers, and ponds. One of the oldest mentioned water spirits - first references date to the Viking Age. The nøkk is a master musician who plays violin or harp to lure people into the water to drown. He is also a shape-shifter who can appear as a handsome young man with long hair (to seduce women), as a monster of twigs and seaweed with glowing eyes (Norwegian tradition), or as a pale grey horse. Despite his malevolent nature, he is often portrayed as lonely and sad, lamenting his inability to receive Christian salvation. The nøkken can be appeased with offerings of black animals, three drops of blood, or brandy - in return, he will tune your fiddle to play as beautifully as his own. Water lilies in his pond are called nøkkerose (nøkk's rose)
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Noaidegažži
description: Noaidegažži (also saivogažži) are the helper spirits of the Sami noaidi (shaman), sent to perform tasks, gather information, and fight other noaidi's spirits. These spirits can take the form of birds (saivoloddi), fish (saivoguolli), or reindeer bulls (saivosarvvát — the strongest form). The noaidegažži assist with healing, finding lost people, predicting weather, locating reindeer herds, and combating evil spirits. They were sent out by the noaidi in trance states, often to great distances. The noaidegažži could be inherited from father to son, sold, or given as dowry. A noaidi's power was measured by the number and strength of his noaidegažži. The most powerful noaidegažži was the reindeer bull form (saivosarvvát), which could fight other noaidi's spirits. The tradition of helper spirits represents the Sami understanding of spiritual power as transferable and competitive
source: Norwegian folk belief and ethnographic records of rural traditions.

name: Ntxwj Nyog (Spirit of Death and Sickness)
description: Ntxwj Nyog (also Ndu Nyong or Ntxwj Nyug) is the primordial spirit of sickness, death, and evil in Hmong shamanic mythology. According to Hmong creation myth, Ntxwj Nyog emerged from an unburned egg when the original creators failed to properly destroy all evil in the world. He descended to earth and began devouring human souls, causing sickness and death. The high god Yawm Saub sent the first shaman Siv Yis to combat Ntxwj Nyog, beginning an eternal struggle between the shaman and the death spirit. Ntxwj Nyog is cunning and relentless — he once tricked Siv Yis into unknowingly eating his own son's soul. Despite the shaman's efforts, Ntxwj Nyog can only be temporarily defeated, never permanently destroyed, explaining why death and sickness persist in the world. He represents the Hmong explanation for suffering — an active, malevolent force that must be constantly battled by shamans through ritual and sacrifice. His presence justifies the entire shamanic system
source: Hmong shamanic oral tradition, Hmong folk religion

name: Nuckelavee
description: The Nuckelavee (also Nuckalavee, Knucker) is the most terrifying creature in Orkney folklore — a skinless horse-like centaur from the sea whose breath withers crops and spreads disease. Its name derives from the Orcadian Norn 'knoggelvi' meaning devil of the sea. The nuckelavee has the torso of a man fused to the back of a horse-like body, with all its muscles, sinews, veins, and organs exposed because it has no skin. Its single red eye burns like fire and its mouth gapes with no lips. The creature emerges from the sea during prolonged dry spells or when water is polluted, bringing drought, plague, and death to livestock. It is particularly associated with the summer months when it rises from the depths to ravage farmland. The only protection against it is running water, which the nuckelavee cannot cross. Burning kelp (seaweed) on the shore is also said to drive it away. During the Victorian cholera epidemics, islanders blamed the nuckelavee for the outbreaks. The creature was so feared that farmers would leave their fields fallow rather than risk encountering it
source: Scottish folklore, collected by John Francis Campbell

name: Nyaminyami (Zambezi River God)
description: Nyaminyami is the most famous river deity in Zambian mythology, the serpent-like god of the mighty Zambezi River. According to Tonga legend, Nyaminyami has the body of a snake and the head of a fish, symbolizing his dominion over both water and land. He is believed to control the flow of the Zambezi River and has the power to either bless or curse the people living along its banks. The legend of Nyaminyami gained international attention during the construction of the Kariba Dam (1955-1959), when the Tonga people warned that damming the river would anger the river god. When the dam faced severe floods and construction delays, many believed Nyaminyami was retaliating. The most dramatic event was the 1957 flood that destroyed the partially built dam wall, an event that entered Zambian national lore. Nyaminyami is still widely venerated by the Tonga people, who hold ceremonies to honor him and seek his protection against natural disasters. The legend represents the deep spiritual connection between the Zambian people and the Zambezi River, one of Africa's greatest waterways
source: Youth Village Zambia; Tonga oral traditions

name: Nykur
description: Nykur is the Icelandic water horse, a shape-shifting water spirit that lures people onto its back and drowns them. Unlike the Norwegian nøkk who uses music, the nykur appears as a beautiful dapple-grey horse with backward-facing hooves and fetlocks that trail water. It stands quietly by rivers, lakes, or the sea, inviting riders. Once mounted, the nykur gallops into the deepest water and drowns its victim. The nykur has one weakness — if someone says its name (nykur), it will flee in terror. It can also be tamed by throwing steel over its head. The nykur can shape-shift into a salmon, a bull, or a fish. Its whinnying is said to be heard in the cracking of winter ice. In some accounts, the nykur can impregnate regular mares, producing half-breed foals that lie down and refuse to move when ridden through belly-deep water, as if remembering their father's nature
source: Icelandic folklore, Íslenzkar þjóðsögur by Jón Árnason

name: Nzazi
description: Nzazi is the powerful spirit of thunder and lightning in Kongo mythology, a fearsome being who patrols the skies during storms hurling bolts of fire at those who break sacred laws. According to tradition, Nzazi was once a man who climbed too high in his ambitions and was transformed into a sky spirit. He patrols the heavens during storms, his flashing eyes creating lightning and his voice thunder. Some traditions describe Nzazi as a canine creature with red or black fur that appears during storms, barks once, and vanishes. Other accounts say Nzazi is accompanied by twelve hounds, with Nzazi representing thunder and the hounds lightning. Trees struck by lightning are said to have been visited by Nzazi's judgment. Survivors of lightning strikes are considered chosen and often become nganga (spiritual healers)
source: Kongo religion — Nzazi is a spirit documented in Kongo oral tradition.

name: Ogou (Lwa of War and Iron)
description: Ogou is the fierce lwa of war, iron, fire, politics, and justice in Haitian Vodou. He is second only to Papa Legba in importance and is the patron of soldiers, blacksmiths, mechanics, drivers, and all who work with metal. Ogou is descended from the Yoruba deity Ogun (god of iron and war), but in Haiti he evolved into a distinct family of lwa including Ogou Feray (the warrior), Ogou Badagris (the politician), and Ogou Balendjo (the healer). He is depicted as a powerful, muscular man dressed in military uniform -- a general coat with epaulettes, a red sash, and a machete or saber. He rides a horse into battle and smokes a cigar. Ogou is syncretized with Saint James the Greater (Santiago Matamoros), depicted as a Moor-slayer on horseback. In the Haitian Revolution, Ogou was the spirit invoked by the revolutionary leaders, and many Haitians believe Ogou fought alongside Dessalines and Louverture. His colors are red and blue. His offerings include raw rum, cigars, grilled corn, roast goat, yams, and machetes or iron objects
source: Haitian Vodou oral tradition, Haiti folklore

name: Old Master
description: Old Master is a recurring character in African American folklore, particularly in the 'trickster slave' narrative cycle. He is the plantation owner (the enslaver) whom clever enslaved protagonists consistently outwit. These stories — collected by Zora Neale Hurston, Julius Lester, and others — portray Old Master not as a benign paternalist but as a figure of arbitrary power who is repeatedly humiliated by the intelligence and wit of those he considers his inferiors. In these tales, the enslaved trickster (often named John or Jack) uses reverse psychology, false deference, and clever wordplay to escape punishment, gain resources, or expose Old Master's hypocrisy. The stories served as coded expressions of resistance, allowing enslaved people to celebrate intellectual triumphs over their oppressors without openly rebelling
source: Charles C. Jones, Negro Myths from the Georgia Coast (1888)

name: Papa Legba (Guardian of the Crossroads)
description: Papa Legba is the foremost lwa (spirit) in Haitian Vodou, serving as the guardian of the crossroads, gateways, and communication between the human world and the realm of the spirits. No ceremony can begin without first invoking Papa Legba, who opens the spiritual gateway. He is an old, wise man who walks with a crutch or cane, often depicted as a humble elder leaning on a staff, wearing a broad-brimmed straw hat and smoking a pipe, carrying a sack or bundle of keys. In Haitian Vodou, he is syncretized with Saint Peter (who holds the keys to heaven) and Saint Lazarus. His origins trace back to the Yoruba deity Elegba/Eshu, but in Haiti he evolved into a gentler, paternal figure who facilitates rather than tests. His colors are red and white, and his sacred day is Monday. Offerings include roasted peanuts, sugarcane, tobacco, coffee, and rum poured at crossroads
source: Haitian Vodou oral tradition, Haiti folklore

name: Pazuzu
description: Pazuzu is a fearsome demonic deity from ancient Assyrian and Babylonian mythology, best known as the personification of the southwestern wind and king of the lilu wind demons. Unlike purely malevolent entities, Pazuzu held a complex dual role in Mesopotamian religion: he brought famine, locusts, storms, and disease through his control of the destructive southwestern wind, yet was also invoked as an apotropaic protector against other malicious spirits. His grotesque image—a hybrid of canine, human, bird, scorpion, and serpent features—was widely used on amulets and statuettes placed in homes and worn by pregnant women to safeguard infants and mothers, particularly against the child-snatching demoness Lamashtu. He was considered the son of Hanbi, king of the underworld demons, and brother to Humbaba, the guardian of the Cedar Forest in the Epic of Gilgamesh. Pazuzu's image appears in Mesopotamian art from the 8th century BCE through the Seleucid period, and he gained renewed global fame as the possessing demon in William Friedkin's 1973 film The Exorcist
source: World History Encyclopedia, Wikipedia, Journal of Ancient Near Eastern Religions, British Museum collections

name: Perchta
description: Frau Perchta (also Berchta, 'the Bright One') is a powerful winter goddess and guardian of moral order in Alpine Germanic folklore, widely regarded as the southern equivalent of Frau Holle. She belongs to the pre-Christian pantheon of continental Germanic peoples and was once venerated as a white-robed deity who oversaw spinning, weaving, and the domestic virtues. During the twelve Rauhnächte (Rough Nights) between Christmas and Epiphany, Perchta roams the countryside entering homes to judge the behavior of children and servants throughout the year. She rewards the industrious with a small silver coin, but the lazy and disobedient face horrific punishment: she slits open their bellies and stuffs the cavity with straw and stones. Her particular concern is spinning — girls who leave their flax unspun by Twelfth Night face her wrath. Despite Church efforts to demonize her (Luther himself railed against 'Fraw Hulde'), Perchta survives in Alpine Perchtenläufe — processions of Schönperchten and Schiachperchten that continue to this day
source: Alpine folklore; Frau Perchta is a powerful winter goddess and guardian of domestic order.
